name: Refund Map (cross-cutting, Payment + Financial)
summary: Two materially different refund implementations exist. Phase 0.10 unified their ENTRY POINTS but deliberately did not unify their behaviour.

implementations.name: Recorded refund
implementations.updates_booking: yes, to 'refunded' when the refund is full
implementations.null_amount_semantics: not reachable — the amount is always supplied

implementations.name: Legacy gateway-only refund
implementations.route: NONE — PaymentController::refund() has no route entry
implementations.updates_booking: yes, to 'refunded' when the refund is full
implementations.null_amount_semantics: a null amount means FULL refund at the gateway and is sent as no amount key

behavioural_differences: REFUND-A writes a refunds row and a PaymentLog row; REFUND-B writes neither.
REFUND-A requires an amount; REFUND-B treats a missing amount as a full refund.
REFUND-A always sends an explicit paise amount to the gateway; REFUND-B omits the amount key entirely when null.
REFUND-A records the gateway response in refunds.metadata.razorpay_response; REFUND-B keeps no response record.

unification_decision.decision: Route BOTH through RefundPaymentUseCase, but keep each service implementation intact behind it.
unification_decision.rationale: The use case is a thin dispatcher. Collapsing the two implementations into one would have to pick a winner on each of the four differences above, changing observable behaviour on the live path. That is a product decision, not a refactor.

money_handling.gateway_payload: integer paise via Money::toPaise(), matching the legacy (int) round($amount * 100)
money_handling.refunds_table_amount: stored in RUPEES as decimal(12,2), NOT paise — pre-existing and preserved
money_handling.note: The gateway payload and the local row use DIFFERENT units. This is legacy behaviour and is pinned by GoldenPaymentBoundaryTest::test_recorded_refund_writes_row_log_and_partial_status.

status_effects.full_determination: Money::isFullRefund($amount, $payment->amount) — a >= comparison, so an over-payment request is also a full refund

failure_semantics.gateway_exception: Propagates out of the DB::transaction. The refund row, the payment status change, the booking status change and the PaymentLog are ALL rolled back.
failure_semantics.net_effect: No local trace of a failed refund attempt, and no gateway debit, because the gateway call precedes every local write.
failure_semantics.gap: An AMBIGUOUS gateway timeout is not covered: if the gateway debited but the response was lost, the local transaction rolls back and no record exists of a real debit.

architecture_rule_4_violation.rule: External network operations must happen outside DB row locks / transactions.
architecture_rule_4_violation.why_not_fixed: Moving the gateway call outside the transaction would change failure semantics: today a gateway failure leaves no local state, and the gateway has not been debited. Moving the call out risks a debited gateway with no local record if the subsequent DB write fails. That is a redesign of financial failure handling, out of scope for an extraction phase.
architecture_rule_4_violation.recommendation: Handle in a dedicated refund-hardening phase with a gateway idempotency key and a pending-intent record written BEFORE the gateway call.

idempotency.consequence: A client retry after an ambiguous timeout can double-refund.
